newsitem.title: JAPAN: FORECAST - BOJ tankan to show manufacturers upbeat.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - BOJ tankan to show manufacturers upbeat.

text.p: Business sentiment in Japan is expected to show modest improvement in a quarterly survey to be released on April 2, although most of the cheer will likely be confined to the manufacturing sector, economists say.

The results of the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) latest "tankan" survey of corporate sentiment, seen as an important indicator of monetary policy, are unlikely to prompt a quick tightening of the central bank's ultra-easy credit stance, they say.

Economists expect the closely watched diffusion index for major manufacturers to rise slightly. They forecast an improvement to between minus two and plus two in March, compared with minus three in November.
If the index rises above zero it will be the first time it has done so since November 1991. In the last survey, firms expected a rise in March to minus one.
The index represents the percentage of firms which see business conditions as favourable minus those which see them as unfavourable.

Economists said large manufacturers would likely be a little more optimistic on the back of strong output data, but that non-manufacturers would be less happy, hurt by poor performances in the retail sector and other service sectors.

Industrial output has climbed in recent months due in part to a weaker yen, which makes Japanese exports more competitive, and in part to a rush of consumer purchases of large items such as cars ahead of a sales tax rise in April to five percent from three percent.
But the government's bid to increase revenue through raising the sales tax, ending income tax cuts and reining in public works spending is seen hanging over the economy's still young recovery.
As a result, firms across the board will be cautious or pessimistic in their outlook for June, economists said.
Some said companies were right to worry that fiscal tightening could pull the plug on the recovery, but others said this natural caution ignored encouraging signs of strength in the economy.
"The underlying tone of the survey is likely to be more upbeat," said Russell Jones at Lehman Brothers, who saw improvements in figures for supply and demand and labour conditions.

Most agreed, however, that the tax-induced uncertainty would mean the BOJ would hold off on a rate rise for at least several months after April and most did not see a rise until the first quarter of 1998.

The BOJ has kept interest rates at rock bottom since September 1995, when it cut its official discount rate, which it charges on loans to commercial banks, to a record low 0.5 percent. But in the past week market interest rates have risen on speculation that the BOJ may tighten its credit grip by the middle of the year.

Those more pessimistic on prospects for the economy said the market was premature in lifting rates but others, including Andrew Shipley at Schroders Japan, said the bond market was on a "one-way trade".
